1:
What exactly is taken away is the chapter’s first difficulty, and the voices divide over it. The Hebrew sets a masculine and a feminine form of the same word side by side, and Adam Clarke renders the pair the support masculine and the support feminine, meaning every kind of support, great or small, strong or weak; his old English manuscript takes them instead of persons and reads the stalworth and the stronge. John Calvin thinks the change of gender was chosen to express more fully the certainty that supports of every kind would be broken, and he declines to refer the words to persons, since they more properly denote all supports whatever their nature; he leaves open whether the term is limited to food or extended to everything that follows. Charles Ellicott goes further and questions the text itself: the immediate explanation of the phrase as bread and water may be a marginal gloss that has found its way in, and the stay and staff may really be the pillars of the state, the great women as well as the great men named afterwards—though he grants that the seventh verse implies famine, so that the prophet may have meant the complete failure of all resources, material and political together.

John Calvin makes the loss of bread more than a shortage. God takes away the staff of bread in two ways: either he deprives us of victuals, or he takes from the food its power of nourishing, since unless he imparts a hidden virtue to it the greatest abundance will do us no good—the belly may be filled and we shall always be hungry. He also presses the word behold, which he says denotes not only certainty but shortness of time, against those who put the judgment off with the excuse that it will be time enough to think of such calamities when they come. John Gill reads the piled-up divine titles as proof that the speaker is able to execute what he threatens. Matthew Henry sees a church and kingdom grown old and leaning on a staff, and notes but does not adopt the application of the words to the decay of the Jewish nation after the crucifixion, which he found in an ancient writer; he would rather take the verse as a warning to all nations. Clarke, for his part, reads the deportation under Nebuchadnezzar as the event, when all the princes, the mighty men, the craftsmen and the smiths were carried off and none remained but the poorest sort.

The catalogue of props is read as a portrait of a state. Keil and Delitzsch observe that Judah had grown into a military state under Uzziah and Jotham, which is why the list opens with soldiers, and they sort the rest carefully—the captain of fifty as leader of the army’s smallest division, the highly distinguished as those whose personal appearance was welcome and regarded with honour. Ellicott adds a personal note: the prophet is named as the representative of a class, the one to which Isaiah himself belonged and in which he found his chief opponents. The prudent divides them. Ellicott gives the word the definite sense of diviners, men who had a real gift of wisdom but by abusing it had become degenerate prophets. Henry allows the same rendering—those who used unlawful arts, rotten stays that were leaned on all the same—but says it may equally be taken in a good sense. Calvin, noting that the word is used badly elsewhere in Scripture, thinks it good here, of one who penetrates dark matters by acuteness rather than by omens; yet he will not quarrel with those who prefer the magical sense, since it is no absurdity that God should strip a nation even of its sinful helps. John Wesley keeps to the plain sense, that the ancient means one whose wisdom was increased by long experience.
3:
The last names on the list are less obvious than they look. Charles Ellicott takes the captain of fifty from a division in which fifty was all but the smallest unit, and reads the honourable man—literally, eminent in countenance—as his civil counterpart. He then reverses a modern impression: the counsellor and the cunning artificer seem to stand at opposite ends of the social order to us, but the second title means masters in arts, and in the East such men ranked with engineers or artists, which is why the craftsmen and smiths were carried off to Babylon with the men of might while the poor were left behind; the building works of Uzziah, he adds, had given them prominence. Some critics, however, take the word as meaning magician. The eloquent orator he renders skilled in speech, and hesitates over the sense: the received version suggests power over the debates of a popular assembly, but the thought may rather be of one who says the right words at the right time, or of an enchanter with incantations ready at command. John Gill notes only how far the fall goes—not a captain of thousands or hundreds, but not even one of fifty.

The threat of boyish rulers is given a face by nearly everyone. Keil and Delitzsch point out that the king is not expressly named, and say the silence was intentional: he had sunk to the mere shadow of a king, led about in leading strings by the aristocratic party that surrounded him, so that a revived Solomonian glory is followed, as before, by the times of Rehoboam. It is a misfortune for a king to be a child, but twice the misfortune when the magnates who advise him are youngsters in the bad sense. Ellicott prefers to render the word youths and suggests the prophet may glance obliquely at Ahaz, who came to the throne at twenty, and recalls that Manasseh was twelve and Josiah eight. Adam Clarke puts the fulfilment later, in the succession of weak and wicked princes from the death of Josiah to the taking of Zedekiah. John Calvin refuses to keep it to age at all: children here means children in mind and conduct, delicate persons without courage who cannot wield the sword entrusted to them. He allows that even a heathen philosopher saw that no one is fit for public government who has not been prepared for it by God, and distinguishes two ways the punishment falls—sometimes able men stumble like blind men the moment they must act, stunned as with a thunderbolt, and sometimes God removes the capable gradually and gives the reins to those who could not govern a family.

Calvin turns the ruin of order into an argument. A well-regulated commonwealth is a singular gift, in which judges, senators, soldiers, captains, artisans and teachers aid one another; since the prophet threatens their loss as a punishment, those who would banish the sword and all civil government are enemies of the public safety, and those who sap its foundations differ in no respect from wild beasts. He grants war is lawful only as an attempt to obtain peace. Keil and Delitzsch read the oppression as reciprocal, each becoming the tyrant of the other, with insolence replacing the reverence owed to the old by the law of nature, the law of the covenant, and common custom alike. Ellicott calls the picture the worst form of decadence in an Eastern kingdom and compares it with a famous ancient account of a democracy corrupted, adding that it might seem drawn from the Turkey or the Egypt of his own day. Gill sees plain anarchy, every man doing as he pleased as when there was no king in Israel, and applies it to Jerusalem under siege, abounding with robbers and spoilers. John Wesley traces the oppression to the command or the permission of such childish rulers.
6:
The scene of a man pressed to rule is read two opposite ways. Keil and Delitzsch take it as the end of the descent: at length no authorities would be left and even the desire to rule would die out, since despotism is followed by mob-rule and mob-rule by anarchy in the most literal sense, so that whoever owned a coat decent enough to clothe himself in would be asked to govern. They find the phrase about the father’s house no idle trait in the picture, the population having grown so thin and dispirited by hunger that the choice could be settled within a narrow circle. Adam Clarke reads the approach as humble entreaty—taking a man by the garment, the gesture used when ten men lay hold of the skirt of a Jew, and when the first king laid hold of the prophet’s robe—and thinks the case requires a person of eminence, so that a word meaning chief or head has probably dropped from the text, since brother of his father’s house is little better than a tautology. John Calvin takes the same verb the other way: it means to lay hands on a person, and those who want a prince will not use flatteries and entreaties but proceed with disorder and violence to seize on someone and compel him to occupy the throne.

Calvin makes the refusal the measure of the ruin. Ambition normally prevails so far that men contend for power at the hazard of their lives, and no place is so inconsiderable as to lack men willing to rule; man is an animal desirous of honour. Everything is therefore in a deplorable condition when that dignity is not merely despised but obstinately rejected, and worse that it is refused not to foreign nations but to kinsmen throwing themselves on his protection. He notes too that princes are commonly chosen for their wealth, so the excuse proves that even the well-off decline. On the oath he says a man who merely excuses himself may yet yield to entreaty, but one who refuses on oath shuts out all hope. The word for healer he takes from surgery—it literally means to bind up, so the answer is I will not be one who binds up your wounds—and reports the alternative that makes the healer a teacher in school or synagogue prescribing what should be done and avoided, but prefers the wound. John Wesley puts it plainly, a repairer of the ruins of the state.

Clarke explains the excuse about bread and clothing by custom rather than poverty. A traveller reports that Eastern households gathered immense stocks of furniture and clothes because their fashions never altered, and that the kings of Persia kept wardrobes of hundreds of habits sorted and ready for presents; the daily provision for the household of Solomon was proportionately great, and even Nehemiah in strait circumstances fed a hundred and fifty at his table. The man is pleading that he has not the means to support the dignity by the liberality and hospitality custom required of his rank. When the cause of the ruin is named, Clarke turns textual critic again: the word rendered eyes is of doubtful form in the printed editions and manuscripts, and he would read cloud, as one ancient version does, alluding to the cloud in which the glory appeared above the tabernacle—though he allows that either reading gives a very good sense. Charles Ellicott keeps the received word and calls it bold anthropomorphic language for the manifestation of God as all-knowing, almighty and all-holy. Calvin presses the same phrase morally: what aggravates the crime is that things done before our eyes offend us most, and these men sinned openly and shamelessly in the very presence of the majesty they defied. John Gill ties the two halves together, that the government was refused because there was no probability of recovering them.
9:
The word behind the show of their countenance is rare, and the voices work at it. John Gill notes it occurs only in this place and reports a derivation from the verb to know, giving the knowledge of their countenance—that is, what may be read off their faces. Keil and Delitzsch refuse a proposal that would make the word mean impudence outright on the strength of a cognate root meaning to stare, and keep the plain sense that their enmity was shamelessly stamped on their features without even the self-condemnation that leads other men to conceal a sin. Adam Clarke quotes a rendering that gives the steadfastness of the countenance and turns it into an image: the eye is the index of the mind, and envy, hatred and malice look intelligently out of it, so that these faces serve the same office as the sonorous rings in the tail of the rattlesnake—they announce the presence of the destroyer. John Calvin makes the point forensic. The prophet had to do with brazen hypocrites who boasted they were good men, and he says their countenance bears testimony, so that no witnesses need be fetched from a distance; disguise their faces as they may, God compels them to carry a mark of their deceit in the forehead. Calvin knows another explanation—that their crimes are so manifest they cannot help seeing in a mirror the baseness they wish to hide—but prefers the first, since what follows is that they publish the sin.

On the comparison itself Charles Ellicott is careful. He thinks it probably earlier in date than the like comparison at the opening of the book, and dates it to a reign in which there was not even the homage vice pays to virtue by feigning a virtue it has not; whether the resemblance is general, in luxury and profligacy of life, or more definite and horrible, he leaves undecided. Matthew Henry presses the moral: shame, which should have restrained them, was thrown off, and this hardens men against repentance as much as anything, for those past shame are past grace and then past hope. He also insists that the injury is inward—sinners may prosper in their outward estates and there still be a woe to their souls, and whatever evil befalls them is of their own procuring. John Wesley says only that they act it publicly, casting off all fear of God and reverence to men.

The word to the righteous is textually the most uncertain thing in the chapter. Clarke calls the reading very dubious, notes that the oldest Greek version has something else entirely at this point, and canvasses conjectures that would give bless ye, or say ye, blessed is; he then defines the righteous by four marks and lists seven conditions in which it shall be well with him, in prosperity and adversity, sickness and health, death, judgment, and through eternity. Calvin approaches it differently. Since severe punishments are a sharp temptation to pious minds, and hardly any public calamity spares the good, the prophet is recalling them to a providence that never confounds anything; and the verb to say, he argues, here means to hold as settled, so that the prophet does not bid anyone tell the righteous man anything but bids every man be fully convinced that his condition will be prosperous though he appear miserable. Calvin takes the two contrasted words as happy and wretched conditions rather than as virtue and wickedness, and rejects a rival construction as forced. Keil and Delitzsch likewise refuse the rendering praise the righteous, since the verb never means to praise but to declare. Gill observes that God always has some righteous ones in the worst of times and can single them out, and Wesley reads the charge as given to the priests. Henry sums up the rule as certain whatever the state of the nation.
11:
The woe on the wicked is where John Calvin states the problem the whole passage answers. When an uncommonly severe calamity falls on all without discrimination, we begin to doubt whether the world is governed by providence or by blind chance; godly men dread that the destruction overtaking the wicked will ruin them too, while others conclude it makes no difference whether a man is good or bad, since both are visited by pestilence, war and famine alike—and out of that gloom, he says, carnal appetites lead many to despair. The prophet therefore asserts that the judgment is right, and asks his hearers to ascribe to God the praise of justice rather than imagine that he punishes with blind violence. Calvin then turns the charge round: the people were suffering the punishment of their crimes and hardening themselves under it as though devoid of feeling, and nothing worse can befall us than to be hardened against chastisement and not perceive who is chastising. Adam Clarke compresses the same verse into a phrase—in a single word say to him, evil—and adds that all is evil in him, before him, after him, above and below him. John Gill reports a second rendering, woe to the wicked, evil, that would make the word a description of the man as exceedingly bad, the chief of sinners, such as the men of Sodom were.

The next verse is contested down to its vocabulary. Keil and Delitzsch work over the word for children and reject two proposals—that it means maltreaters or triflers, since despotic treatment is already contained in the word for oppressors, and that it means a suckling, since it occurs elsewhere alongside the word for suckling and so cannot mean the same thing. Their conclusion is that it names the boy as playful and wanton: boys at their games. Clarke attacks the other end of the verse. The word rendered cause thee to err literally means swallow, and he canvasses three emendations offered for it, giving confound, disturb and trouble, before setting out a reading of the whole verse that changes it altogether—the collectors of grapes shall be their oppressors, and usurers, by a change of vowels in the word for women, shall rule over them.

On the sense the voices are nearer together. Charles Ellicott refers the children back to the youth and still more to the character of Ahaz, in whose counsels the influence of the queen-mother and the seraglio was dominant—a cowardly and idolatrous king delighting in foreign worships and foreign forms of art—and notes that the evil worked downwards from the throne until princes, priests and judges were all drifting with the current. Calvin makes the submission itself the punishment. Men are never more reluctant than to have a yoke laid on them, so feeble and cowardly must the minds be that obey delicate rulers and let themselves be oppressed by them; those who offer their shoulders like asses have been struck by God with a spirit of cowardice, and it is their peculiar reproach that while they obstinately shake off the yoke of God they yield abject service to men. He also weighs a rival rendering of the leaders, since the participle may come from a root meaning to call happy, and the old Greek version reads it so. Calvin allows that false prophets did flatter the people, but sees no reason why flatteries should be mentioned at this point, and prefers to keep the rulers themselves as the cause of the ruin: princes are raised to office for the public safety, and no plague is more destructive than when bad men hold it and govern by their own caprice, since it was their business to correct others and to show the way by their own example. John Wesley glosses briefly, that the women are weak and effeminate rulers and the misleaders are the rulers civil and ecclesiastical alike.
13:
The court scene is described with unusual precision. Keil and Delitzsch sort out the postures: when God, weary with his long-suffering, rises from his heavenly throne that is called standing up; when he assumes the judgment-seat in sight of all the world that is called sitting down; and when, having come down, he comes forward as accuser, that is standing, with the added idea of being firm and ready. They add that the pleading is also judging, because an accusation that cannot be contradicted contains the sentence within itself. They also read the object as the nations rather than the people, while Adam Clarke notes that the old Greek version reads his people. Charles Ellicott catches the rhetorical turn: the people may think the prophet is their censor, and he bids them know that the Lord is their true accuser and judge, then swings round with a sudden change of person as if facing the nobles. John Calvin explains why the scene is needed. So long as wickedness rages unchecked and no relief comes from above, we think God idle and forgetful of his duty, and when the nobles are spared he seems to grant them liberty to sin, as though they were sacred persons not to be touched. John Gill reads the whole pleading of a much later quarrel, the cause of the Son against those who rejected him.

The charge against the elders is broken off before it begins. Keil and Delitzsch observe that the divine speech opens with and ye, the clause it answers being left unsaid—something like, I set you over my vineyard—and they argue the suppression is God’s own and not the prophet’s, since the majesty with which he appeared was itself proof of what he had entrusted to them. Calvin adds a lexical observation, that the verb ordinarily meaning to burn does not suit a passage about men making a profit of what they consume, so it should be taken of eating down the produce as cattle eat down grass. He presses the treachery of it: these were the vine-dressers, and instead of cultivating the vine they devoured it like wild beasts. He also names the immunity they claimed—their rank set them beyond reproof, and heathen princes might be called to account but not they—and answers that the palace of princes ought to resemble a sanctuary, so that it is the grossest sacrilege to turn one into a den of thieves. Clarke prefers the reading my vineyard, on the authority of three ancient versions, and John Wesley notes that the ancients are the rulers, commonly chosen out of men in ripe years, who destroyed what they were set to preserve.

The closing question is left deliberately unanswered. Gill reads the beating to pieces as reduction to the utmost poverty. Clarke calls the image of grinding faces strong, then says it is exceeded by another prophet, and quotes the passage that has the rulers tearing the skin from the people and the flesh from their bones, chopping them asunder as morsels for the pot—where he also proposes an emendation by transposing a single letter, following two old versions. Calvin makes the interrogation the point: to whom shall the poor betake themselves but to the magistrate, who ought to be the father of his country and the protector of the wretched? The vehemence conveys that the accusation comes not from men but from God, who will at length take vengeance; and since men raised to honour disdain all direction, the prophet meets their pride by setting the divine majesty against it. Calvin closes with an argument from the greater to the less: no one can escape that arm, for if God punishes even the princes, he will hardly spare the lowest of the people.
16:
Everyone notices the change of target, and two of them defend it. John Wesley observes that the prophet had hitherto reproved the men. Matthew Henry says the prophet expressly vouches God’s authority for what follows, lest it be thought unbecoming in him to take notice of such things: whether they hear or forbear, God is much displeased with the folly and vanity of proud women, and his law takes cognizance even of their dress. Charles Ellicott calls the passage without parallel in the minuteness of its detail—it is as though the prophet had gone into the boudoir of a leader of fashion and taken an inventory of what he found—and counts twenty-one articles whose names mostly carry a foreign stamp, luxury having imported its novelties so that the women of Judah took up the fashions of Tyre or Damascus. John Calvin explains why the indictment starts where it does. Had the prophet begun with dress and gait, it would have been easy to answer that the mind was still pure and some elegance of clothing hardly warranted such bitter language; so he begins at the fountain, laying open the inward disease of pride that the dress only manifests.

One word divides them sharply. Adam Clarke renders it falsifying their eyes, meaning setting them off falsely with paint, and says the traditional pointing arose from confusing it with a root connected with the mineral used to colour the eyes. He then piles up evidence for the custom: a traveller’s description of his wife’s long lashes, dressed after the fashion of the East, giving a dark and majestic shade to the eyes; the black powder women put between the lid and the eye with a fine long pencil, which sets off the whiteness of the eye and is said to comfort the sight; an ancient naturalist on the same mineral as dilating the eyes and healing ulcerations of the lid; a satirist on a man lengthening his eyebrow with an oblique bodkin. Calvin reports both derivations and rejects the painting one, since the prophet’s object here is to describe not ornaments but affected motions of the body; unchaste eyes, he says, are the heralds of an unchaste heart, while chaste eyes are sedate and not wandering. On the tinkling Ellicott is confident—small silver bells were fastened at the ankles, so the beauties of the city carried their music with them, and the custom survives still. Calvin is not: he cannot tell whether they wore something on their sandals that made a noise or imitated dancing women by a measured step, dress having changed so greatly, though he adopts the noise as the plainer sense.

The sentence itself is read two ways. Ellicott divides it: partly diseases such as leprosy, causing baldness, engendered by misery and captivity, and partly the brutal outrage of the invaders who stripped off the costly garments and left the wearers naked. Clarke dwells on the second, noting that conquerors of that age stripped their captives and made them travel so, exposed to the weather and the intolerable heat of the sun, always mentioned as the hardest part of a captive’s lot and the height of indignity to women whose faces had scarcely been seen; he also prefers a reading of three old versions giving will humble rather than will smite. John Gill keeps the correspondence exact, the scab answering to the binding and plaiting and curling of the hair, which must now fall out or be shaven off. Keil and Delitzsch look ahead to the inventory and offer renderings throughout—ankle-clasps, crescents, arm-chains, stepping-chains, smelling-bottles, amulets, gala-dresses, hand-mirrors—pointing to two specialist works. Calvin declines the task outright: the best Hebrew scholars have doubts about some of these things and cannot distinguish their forms with certainty, and it is enough to see the design of heaping them up.
18:
The inventory sets the commentators three different tempers. John Wesley takes the shortest road: it is agreed by all that these were ornaments of the time, and it is of no concern to understand their differences exactly. Adam Clarke takes the longest, and often fails at the end of it. On the ankle ornaments he reports that the root means to skip, to bound, to dance along, and that the things named were chains or rings that tinkled as the wearer moved nimbly; a traveller he cites saw women of the first rank in silver bands at wrist and foot, hung with little silver rings that clatter like a cymbal as they walk. John Gill canvasses three quite different explanations of the same word: fetters, since the term elsewhere means stocks; golden chains fastened to both feet that directed the walk and kept the wearer from too large a step; or plates of gold, one to four fingers broad, set about the ankles of infants in wealthy families, not for noise or restraint but for ornament and to distinguish them from the meaner sort.

The next two items show how far the difficulty goes. Clarke refuses a scholar’s rendering of the cauls as little sun-shaped studs answering to the crescents that follow, since it depends on an exchange of letters he knows no instance of in Hebrew; then reports that his friend searched the Arabic dictionaries, printed and in manuscript, and found neither the word nor anything belonging to it, so no help was to be had there either. Charles Ellicott gives the same two options without deciding hard between them—probably wreaths or plaits of gold or silver network worn over the forehead from ear to ear, though some scholars take them for sun-like balls worn as a necklace—and identifies the crescents with the ornaments hung on the camels of the Midianite kings in the time of Gideon, still worn by Arabian women, not improbably tied once to the worship of Ashtaroth and now kept as a charm against the evil eye. On the chains Gill and Ellicott simply part: Gill reports drop bottles of gold hung at the neck with balsam in them, or else chains strung with small stones of bdellium, while Ellicott says the word means earrings.

Three of the remaining items are disputed outright. Clarke insists that the nose jewels are literally that—rings set with jewels hanging from bored nostrils—and calls the rival explanation, which makes them strings of pearl hanging from the forehead to the top of the nose, nothing short of ridiculous, citing the proverb about a jewel of gold in a swine’s snout to prove the custom old; Wesley, undisturbed, glosses them as fastened to the head and hanging down the forehead to the beginning of the nose. Ellicott reads the crisping pins as purses, small embroidered bags attached to the girdle, and calls them a refinement of female luxury, the girdle itself serving men for a purse; Wesley takes them for pins of silver or gold used to curl the hair. On the glasses, Wesley notes that they were not glass at all but bright and burnished brass, and Ellicott agrees they are polished metal mirrors carried in the hand; but Gill reports the same authority giving elsewhere thin garments, so called because the flesh is seen through them, the sense the old Greek version took, and Ellicott admits the curiosity of that rendering as throwing light on the social life of Alexandria, if not of Israel. Clarke describes that gauze as worn only by women who dressed more elegantly than modest women should, showing not merely the shape of the body but the colour of the skin. Ellicott ends by noticing the direction of the catalogue, the prophet carrying his eye upward from the feet to the head, and remarks that neither stockings nor handkerchiefs appear in it.
24:
The reversal is set out clause by clause. Charles Ellicott reads it as a slave-march: for the perfume of the scent-bottles the stench of squalor and pestilence; for the embroidered girdle not a rent but the rope they would be dragged along by; for plaited hair the baldness of those cropped as slaves were cropped; for the cloak a scanty tunic of coarse sackcloth. John Calvin lingers on the perfumes. The country abounded in aromatic herbs, and since nations far from the east are not deterred by distance or expense from that luxury, what is to be expected where such things are plentiful? Ointments, he concludes, were abused in a variety of ways, the desires of men being ingenious and never satisfied; and he draws the moral that both sexes are to make sober use of God’s gifts, since extravagance cannot be restrained by a lighter chastisement. Adam Clarke supplies the background. Much of the delicacy of these households lay in baths and the richest oils, and he recalls the year-long preparation of one queen before she was presented, six months with oil of myrrh and six with sweet odours—so that a loathsome body in place of a skin softened by every art was the most mortifying punishment possible. John Gill traces the stench to ulcers and disease, and notes three versions reading dust.

The last clause is the most damaged in the chapter, and everyone handles it differently. Ellicott takes the burning for a brand stamped on the flesh, often on the forehead, marking them as the slaves of their captors. Calvin takes it for sunburn, observing that fashionable women hardly dare expose themselves to the sun for fear of it, and that this is exactly what will happen; John Wesley agrees, adding that they had guarded against it with the utmost care. Clarke goes further and doubts the text. He reports a scholar who thought two of the words an interpolation because one old version omits them, and holds instead that the clause is imperfect at its end: the word taken as a noun for burning is without example, the sentence breaks off abruptly, and the best Greek manuscripts show the same marks of imperfection there. The gap, from the loss of probably three or four words, he judges of long standing, and offers a restoration giving, instead of beauty thou shalt have an ill-favoured countenance.

The address then changes. Keil and Delitzsch note that the prophet turns from the daughters of Zion to the daughter of Zion herself, who loses her sons and so leaves her daughters without husbands, and that thy might stands for thy men. Calvin gives another reason for the shift: it would be improper to assign more than one husband to one woman, so the words must be spoken to the city rather than the women. Clarke notes a manuscript variant here. On the closing picture the voices converge and then divide over its date. Keil and Delitzsch see the gates where the husbands once gathered turned to desolation, and the city brought down from her lofty seat to the ground—exactly as the province is figured on Roman medals struck after the city fell, a woman utterly broken beneath a palm tree in an attitude of despair. Clarke describes one such coin from his own collection and quotes a writer who thought the engravers had an eye on the customs of the nation; but his note objects that the passage relates, in its nearer view at least, to the destruction under Nebuchadnezzar and the captivity at Babylon, while Gill refers the falling by the sword to the Romans. Calvin keeps to the plain sense, that where there were great crowds there will be dismal solitude; he does not deny the figure of a widow bewailing her loss, but the sum of the matter is that the city will have lost her inhabitants.
